title: Opportunistic infections
question: Assign the ICD-10-CM code for the patient's infection (only that code).
note:
Chief Complaint
Oral white patches and discomfort.

HPI
The patient is an 86-year-old male who presents today for an evaluation of white patches on his tongue. He reports that the spots appeared several weeks ago following the initiation of a long-term inhaled steroid regimen for respiratory management. He notes that the patches are mildly irritating but does not report any significant difficulty with his diet. He states that he is able to swallow his food and liquids normally without any obstruction or discomfort. He is seeking treatment to clear the white plaques.

Medication List
- Inhaled corticosteroid
- Lisinopril 10mg daily
- Atorvastatin 20mg daily

Review of Systems
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or fatigue.
HEENT: Reports white patches on the tongue; no sore throat or ear pain.
Respiratory: Occasional wheezing; no shortness of breath.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling.
Neurological: No dizziness or numbness.

Social History
The patient resides at home with his wife. He is a retired engineer and enjoys gardening. He denies tobacco or alcohol use.

Family History
Father had hypertension. Mother had a history of heart disease.

Vitals
Blood Pressure: 138/82 mmHg
Heart Rate: 74 bpm
Respiratory Rate: 16 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 97% on room air
Temperature: 98.4 F
Height: 5'10"
Weight: 175 lbs

Recent Labs
eGFR: 72 mL/min/1.73m2
HbA1c: 5.8%
TSH: 2.1 mIU/L

Exam
General: The patient is alert and in no acute distress.
Oral Cavity: Examination of the oral mucosa reveals prominent white plaques on the tongue and inner buccal mucosa. The plaques are consistent with oral candidiasis. The mucosa is otherwise healthy.
Neck: No lymphadenopathy noted.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.

Assessment
The patient has developed thrush as a side effect of his chronic inhaled steroid use. His swallowing remains intact and functional.

Plan
1. Prescribe Nystatin oral rinse to be used four times daily for 7 to 14 days.
2. Instruct the patient to rinse and spit after each use.
3. Monitor for resolution of the white plaques.
4. Continue current medications as prescribed.

Electronically signed,
P. O'Brien, PA-C
May 14, 2026
explanations: Oral thrush: candidal stomatitis, B37.0 (no HCC).
